name: Retail
blurb: Demand forecasting, recommendation, and customer-service automation at volume, with NRF, Coresight, and IHL tracking the deployments.

points.desc: The Census BTOS series reports AI use for retail trade alongside every other sector, updated fortnightly.
points.name: Adoption is measured, not guessed

points.desc: The National Retail Federation covers store automation, inventory computer vision, and customer-experience software - the trade body's research is where retail AI adoption gets counted.
points.name: NRF tracks store technology

points.desc: Retail research firm producing adoption rates and market sizing for AI in merchandising and supply-chain logistics.
points.name: Coresight sizes the market

points.desc: IHL Group tracks retail technology expenditure and operational return across grocery, apparel, and general merchandise.
points.name: IHL measures the software spend

summary: Demand forecasting, recommendation, and customer-service automation are the volume use cases.

analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Business Outlook Survey puts AI use in retail trade at 15.2 percent of firms in the most recent period, a figure essentially flat with the prior reading of 15.5 percent, suggesting that adoption has reached a plateau among early movers rather than continuing to climb steeply. The survey asks only whether a business used AI in the past two weeks, so it captures active deployment rather than stated intention, making it a conservative but credible baseline for the sector.

Where retail AI is actually being applied, the picture emerging from industry trackers is broad. IHL Group highlights demand forecasting and replenishment as a concentrated area of investment, pointing to cases such as Amart Furniture's adoption of RELEX Solutions' AI-native platform across 66 stores and four distribution centers to forecast demand, optimize purchase orders, and adjust for supplier lead-time variability. IHL Group also flags that inventory distortion has fallen to 1.7 trillion dollars globally, though empty shelves still account for 690.9 billion dollars in losses, and notes that AI agents are increasingly being deployed in real-time to address those gaps rather than waiting on periodic planning cycles.

Customer-facing applications are receiving parallel attention. David's Bridal, as reported by IHL Group, rebuilt its Pearl AI assistant to help shoppers plan weddings through AI-generated vision boards drawing on 75 years of company data and stylist expertise, serving both in-store teams and third-party vendors such as photographers and florists. Coresight Research, which focuses on retail and technology intersections, frames personalization, retail media, and what it calls unified commerce as the central themes reshaping grocery and broader retail, with category management and private-label strategy among the functions being retooled around data science and AI.

On the question of where money and attention concentrate, IHL Group's own headline from mid-2026 is pointed: most retail AI budgets are funding the wrong layer first, and that misallocation is stalling pilots before they reach the store floor. That observation matters for any operator evaluating deployment, because it implies that technical infrastructure choices, rather than algorithm quality, are the primary constraint on realizing returns. NRF echoes a related concern, framing its 2026 agenda around how retailers can move AI initiatives beyond experimentation by building the internal culture, influence, and trust those programs require.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the aggregate picture is one of genuine but uneven progress. A measured adoption rate just above 15 percent means that most retail firms are not yet active users, leaving competitive room but also meaning that proven playbooks are still being written. The clearest ROI signals in the available material cluster around supply-chain and procurement functions, where Kimberly-Clark's rollout of an AI-powered procurement platform achieved 40 to 50 percent improvement in knowledge-search productivity according to IHL Group, and where inventory forecasting tools have measurable impact on availability and working capital. Customer-experience applications show ambition but fewer hard numbers. The sources are largely silent on regulatory posture specific to retail AI, so that dimension warrants separate investigation before committing to deployment at scale.
